items.title: GitHub Desktop adds short-lived authentication tokens
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: When you sign in to GitHub Desktop 3.6.10 or later, eligible accounts can now use short-lived, automatically refreshing authentication tokens. Short-lived access tokens reduce how long a leaked token can be used. Desktop automatically refreshes them for GitHub API requests and Git operations, keeping token renewal out of your everyday workflow. We’re rolling this out gradually on github.com, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud, so it isn’t available to everyone yet. This token rollout doesn’t include GitHub Enterprise Server. items.title: CodeQL 2.27.3 adds Python 3.15 features and JSON data extensions
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: CodeQL is the static analysis engine behind GitHub code scanning, which finds and remediates security issues in your code. We’ve recently released CodeQL 2.27.3. It supports new Python 3.15 language features, adds JSON syntax for data extensions, adds C23 bit-precise integers, and includes accuracy improvements across languages. Language and framework support CodeQL CLI Data extension files now support JSON syntax, using the same structure as YAML data extensions. Java-style comments (// ... and /* ... */) also work. CodeQL parses files with the .json extension as JSON and continues to parse all other files as YAML. We’ve added an opt-in ai threat model for LLM-generated data. It doesn’t include any built-in source models, so you can define your own sources with data extensions. Python The Python extractor now supports Python 3.15 syntax, including unary plus in match literal patterns and Unicode 17 identifiers. We’ve added support for the new frozendict and sentinel builtins introduced in Python 3.15, including data flow modeling for frozendict construction. C/C++ We’ve added support for C23 bit-precise integers (_BitInt(N)). We’ve added flow summaries for the BlazingMQ BloombergLP::bmqa::Message and MessageProperties classes and their iterators. C# We’ve added support for data flow through positional patterns in is expressions and switch cases. When you configure private registries, CodeQL now passes the required proxy and certificate environment variables to the NuGet CLI. Ruby CodeQL now treats Grape::API request sub-accessors as remote flow sources. These include body.read, body.string, params, GET, POST, cookies, env, query_string, and path_info. Query changes C/C++ The cpp/resource-not-released-in-destructor query now recognizes resources released through local aliases, reducing false positives. C# The cs/simplifiable-boolean-expression query now produces fewer false positives when type information is incomplete. Java/Kotlin The java/ssrf and java/unvalidated

items.title: Look up a resource’s cost center with the GitHub REST API
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now use the GitHub REST API to find which cost center a user, organization, repository, or enterprise team belongs to. Previously, you had to list every cost center and scan its resources. Pass the resource type and name to the new endpoint. The response includes the cost center’s ID and name. items.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines, we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago, which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears: Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of (very small) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do, 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction (possible overstatement here), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot, beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has n
items.why_it_matters: Research on LLMs reading and writing model weights has no near-term delivery impact, but the market notes (Anthropic bond rating, OpenAI fundraising) are worth watching for vendor risk.

items.title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.author: Basil Chatha
items.excerpt: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube →Open video on YouTube ↗What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not wh

items.title: llm 0.37
items.excerpt: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna. LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721, ac1982, Allen Flux, Bian Yuhan, Bishop Kammeraad, Chen Yufeiyang, Christopher Krah, Ethan Stoner, Jiachen Xie, Olamide Faniyan, Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu, nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release! Tags: open-source, projects, ai, annotated-release-notes, generative-ai, llms, embeddings, llm

items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.excerpt: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Weight-Space Programming Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming. The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update
